# Brief: David (PERSONA-002)
## Upcoming Meeting: 2026-05-05

# Brief: David — May 5, 2026

## Since Last Meeting

The school board advanced the FY27 budget to the city council on a 4-2 vote at the April 14 presentation. The budget is built to the 6% local tax ceiling — approximately $257/year for the average homeowner, 3.3% overall growth. Health insurance finalized at 5.14% (releasing $655K against the 11.5% ceiling). Kaler closure (6-1) and Option A reconfiguration (4-2) are authorized.

The city manager's position paper accompanying the presentation documented the statutory boundary: the council may only adjust the total appropriation figure, not direct which positions or programs are affected. This means the May 5 hearing is a binary-or-scaling decision — accept the 6% figure, reduce it, or reject it.

No new evidence has emerged between the April 14 presentation and this hearing. The three-week gap is standard administrative lead time before a council appropriation vote. The district has not posted updated budget materials on the budget27 page, introduced FY26 closing data, or released the implementation cost estimates for elementary reconfiguration. The FY25 audit findings ($2.37M unauthorized overspending, $600K under-withheld benefits) have not received a formal board remediation commitment on the public record since being introduced by a community member on April 7.

The operative question remains the one you flagged at the April 14 handoff: will the council accept 6%, or reduce the figure and trigger a revision cycle with fewer than five weeks before the June 9 referendum?

## Open Questions

- What does the combined property tax burden actually look like when the school 6% increase, Pearl Street's 22% annual sewer rate hikes (doubling bills by FY29), the November public safety bond ($80–87M), and the deferred Mahoney renovation ($70–76M, November 2027) are modeled together? No institution has produced this analysis — and Councilor Matthews' March 19 dissent is still the only on-record signal that anyone on either body is doing the cross-budget math.
- What is the full dollar magnitude of the reserve accounts carrying negative balances? A complete accounting could change the district's actual net financial position relative to what was presented in budget workshops.
- Are the $2.37M in unauthorized FY25 overspending and $600K in under-withheld employee benefits receiving a formal board remediation commitment, or do they remain in the public comment record without an official response?
- Did the unverified state aid figures ($300K targeted aid, $750K EPS formula change) that drove the April 2 budget deferral turn out to be real and recurring — or are they one-year windfalls that will compound the FY28 gap when they disappear?
- Is the SRO budget line ($221K on the city's estimate, unverified by the district) subject to the same correction-to-actual discipline Ketchem applied to electricity and tuition reimbursement — or does its cross-governmental sourcing exempt it from that scrutiny?
- What are the actual reconfiguration implementation costs (transportation routing, building compliance, IEP transitions) and do they fit within the $179K contingency — or is that figure already consumed by items we haven't seen itemized?
- What is the dollar magnitude of untracked SPTA time-beyond-contract hours, and what mechanism absorbs those costs when they hit given a fund balance at or below zero?
- What other line items in the approved FY26 budget were understated by a factor similar to the nutrition fund (budgeted at $202K against a deficit several times that)?
- Does the board have a plan to contain benefits cost growth if health insurance continues rising — noting that FY27 already showed a $294K surge in transportation driver and clerk benefits alone?
- When will the board adopt a specific fund balance reserve target with a multi-year rebuild timeline? The 9% benchmark (~$6.75M) is on the record, and the 1% contingency seed vote was unanimous, but no formal dollar target or rebuild schedule has been adopted.
- What does a balanced FY28 budget actually require if EPS formula changes are unfavorable — given labor auto-escalation above 6%, 13–14% annual utility inflation, $300K+ in new debt service, and a fund balance starting at zero or below?

## Agenda Implications

No agenda is available for this meeting. However, the May 5 council appropriation hearing is the statutory mechanism by which the council acts on the school budget. The hearing format is predictable even without an agenda: public comment, council deliberation on the appropriation figure, and a vote. The following guidance applies regardless of agenda specifics:

**What this means for you specifically**: This is the single most consequential meeting of the budget cycle for the 6% ceiling you've been tracking since December. The council can accept, reduce, or reject the appropriation. A reduction triggers a board revision cycle with fewer than five weeks before the June 9 referendum — a calendar constraint the board has not publicly gamed out. A rejection is procedurally possible but unlikely; a reduction to 3–5% would push required cuts back toward the $8–9M range that the February 10 joint workshop implied but the board never fully modeled.

**What to listen for**: Whether any councilor raises the FY25 audit findings or the negative reserve balances as a condition of appropriation approval — particularly whether the material weakness finding (second consecutive year) prompts a request for a remediation timeline with measurable milestones before the FY27 budget is finalized. Track whether Councilor Matthews builds on her March 19 dissent by connecting the school appropriation to the other capital obligations. Listen for whether the city manager or any councilor asks about the unverified state aid assumptions embedded in the budget the board passed.

**Questions to prepare**: If you speak (public comment or private conversation), your highest-value contribution is the integrated taxpayer impact question that no one has asked: "Has the city produced a combined projection showing what the average homeowner's total bill looks like across the school budget, Pearl Street sewer rates, the public safety bond if it passes in November, and the Mahoney renovation when it comes in 2027? If not, how does the council make this appropriation decision without understanding the full load on the same property tax base?"

## Watch For

- **Councilor Matthews**: She was the lone 6-1 dissent on Pearl Street, explicitly naming school layoffs and cross-budget math. Does she extend that analysis to the appropriation vote? Her statement is the best signal of whether the combined fiscal picture is entering council deliberation.
- **Whether any councilor asks about the FY25 audit findings**: The $2.37M unauthorized overspending and $600K under-withheld benefits were introduced by a community member, not the administration. If a councilor raises them during deliberation, it signals the council is treating financial controls as a condition of the appropriation, not a separate governance issue.
- **The specific appropriation figure if the council reduces from 6%**: A reduction to 5% shifts approximately $540K in additional cuts back to the board. A reduction to 4% pushes it past $1M. The precise number matters for the revision cycle calendar and for whether the board can realistically produce a revised budget before June 9.
- **Any councilor asking about the unverified state aid figures**: The $300K targeted aid and $750K EPS formula change drove the April 2 budget deferral but were unverified at the time of the board vote. If the council asks whether these numbers have been confirmed — or whether they're recurring — it reveals whether the council is reading the budget at the same level of detail you are.
- **Public comment from district staff**: If SPTA or SPESPA representatives raise the untracked time-beyond-contract hours or the absence of FTE data for their bargaining units, it confirms the pattern of systemic under-tracking extends beyond the items already documented (nutrition, benefits, electricity, tuition reimbursement).
- **Whether the city manager reiterates or walks back the statutory boundary**: The position paper stated the council may only adjust the total appropriation. If any councilor attempts to condition the appropriation on specific program changes, watch whether the manager holds that line or opens the door to council-directed cuts — either outcome changes the governance dynamic.
- **The FY28 mention test**: Does anyone on the council — or in public comment — ask what a balanced FY28 budget looks like given everything Ketchem named on March 23: labor auto-escalation above 6%, utility inflation, new debt service, and a fund balance at zero? If FY28 is not raised, the institution is making a one-year decision without the multi-year frame you've been building since December.
- **The budget27 materials page**: Before the meeting, check whether spsdme.org/page/budget27 has been updated with the board-approved budget document and supporting data. If the page still contains only workshop-stage materials, the public voting June 9 cannot reconstruct the full fiscal picture from a single source — a gap that becomes the council's problem if they approve without addressing it.
